name: Arabic: Levantine (Shami) for speaking, MSA for reading
ttsNote: The built-in iOS Arabic voice speaks MSA. Levantine lines are read with MSA sounds (e.g. ق as q, not the glottal stop Shami speakers use), so treat dialect audio as an approximation. Use 'Add a speaker' to record a native speaker.

translit.name: Simplified: ʔ = glottal stop, ʕ = ʿayn, ḥ ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ = emphatic/pharyngeal, ā ī ū ē ō = long vowels

frequency.source: FrequencyWords by Hermit Dave (OpenSubtitles 2018, Arabic), CC BY-SA 4.0
frequency.note: Subtitle Arabic is mostly MSA with some dialect, so this estimates coverage of MSA-leaning real text.

notes.title: Why Levantine + MSA (diglossia)
body: Arabic speakers talk in a dialect and read/write in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Speaking MSA in a café sounds like quoting Shakespeare at a barista.

This pack teaches **Levantine (Shami: Damascus/Beirut)** for speaking and listening from day 1, and **MSA** for reading from Unit 10. Words show their MSA form when it differs, so the two grow together.
Everything you write in Arabic script transfers: the alphabet, roots and most vocabulary are shared.

notes.title: ق in Shami
body: City Levantine pronounces ق (q) as a glottal stop ʔ: قهوة is ʔahwe, قلب is ʔalb. MSA keeps q. Transliteration here follows Shami pronunciation; the built-in voice will still say q.

notes.title: Typing Arabic on iPhone
body: Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard → Arabic (free). Switch with the globe key. You can also use the keyboard's dictation microphone to speak an answer instead of typing.

notes.title: Unverified content
body: All Levantine sentences in this pack were written by Claude and are marked unverified. Levantine varies by city and family. If something looks wrong, tap 'Flag' on it; flags are saved and included in your backup so they can be fixed in the pack later.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 1: ا ب ت ث ن ي
scriptLessons.note: Arabic is written right to left. Most letters join to the next one; the dots are what tell ب ت ث ن ي apart in the middle of a word.

letters.name: alif
letters.sound: Long 'a' (father), or a seat for a vowel at the start of a word. Never joins to the next letter.

letters.name: bāʔ
letters.sound: b as in 'bed'. One dot below.

letters.name: tāʔ
letters.sound: Light t (tongue on teeth). Two dots above.

letters.name: thāʔ
letters.sound: MSA: 'th' in 'think'. Shami usually says t or s. Three dots above.

ex.en: three (Shami spells with ت; MSA ثلاثة)

letters.name: nūn
letters.sound: n. One dot above; deep bowl at the end of a word.

letters.name: yāʔ
letters.sound: y as in 'yes', or long ī / ē. Two dots below.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 2: ج ح خ
scriptLessons.note: Same shape, different dots. ح is the most important new sound: a breathy h squeezed from the throat.

letters.name: jīm
letters.sound: Shami: like the s in 'measure' (zh). MSA: j as in 'jam'. Dot below.

letters.name: ḥāʔ
letters.sound: Pharyngeal h: tighten your throat as if fogging a cold window hard. No dot. Not the same as ه.

letters.name: khāʔ
letters.sound: Like Spanish j in 'jamón' or German 'Bach'. Dot above.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 3: د ذ ر ز و
scriptLessons.note: These five never join to the following letter, so words often have gaps.

letters.name: dāl
letters.sound: Light d.

letters.name: dhāl
letters.sound: MSA: 'th' in 'this'. Shami usually d or z.

ex.en: this (Shami spells with د; MSA هذا)

letters.name: rāʔ
letters.sound: Tapped r, like Spanish 'pero'.

letters.name: zāy
letters.sound: z as in 'zoo'.

letters.name: wāw
letters.sound: w, or long ū / ō. Also the word 'and', written joined to the next word.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 4: س ش ص ض
scriptLessons.note: ص and ض are emphatic: say them with the back of the tongue raised; they darken the vowels next to them.

letters.name: sīn
letters.sound: Plain s.

letters.name: shīn
letters.sound: sh as in 'ship'.

letters.name: ṣād
letters.sound: Emphatic s: tongue back, lips slightly rounded; the vowel after it sounds deeper ('saw' rather than 'sat').

letters.name: ḍād
letters.sound: Emphatic d. Arabic is called 'the language of ḍād'.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 5: ط ظ ع غ
scriptLessons.note: ع (ʿayn) is a voiced squeeze in the throat: the hardest sound for English speakers, and essential.

letters.name: ṭāʔ
letters.sound: Emphatic t.

letters.name: ẓāʔ
letters.sound: Emphatic z (MSA: emphatic 'th' of 'this').

letters.name: ʕayn
letters.sound: Tighten the throat like gagging slightly, then voice through it. Not a vowel and not a glottal stop.

letters.name: ghayn
letters.sound: Gargled r, like French 'r' in 'Paris'.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 6: ف ق ك ل
scriptLessons.note: Remember ق is a glottal stop in city Shami, but q in MSA.

letters.name: fāʔ
letters.sound: f. One dot above.

letters.name: qāf
letters.sound: MSA: q from deep in the throat. Shami: glottal stop (the catch in 'uh-oh').

letters.name: kāf
letters.sound: k.

letters.name: lām
letters.sound: Light l. ل + ا is written as one shape: لا.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 7: م ه ة ء + vowel marks
scriptLessons.note: Short vowels are usually not written; learners' texts add them as small marks (harakat). Toggle them in Settings.

letters.name: mīm
letters.sound: m.

letters.name: hāʔ
letters.sound: Ordinary breathy h, as in 'hat'. Lighter than ح.

letters.name: tāʔ marbūṭa
letters.sound: Feminine ending, said -a or -e; becomes -it before a possessor (jāmʕit Hopkins).

letters.name: hamza
letters.sound: Glottal stop. Often sits on a seat: أ إ ؤ ئ.

letters.name: fatḥa
letters.sound: Short a: a small stroke above.

letters.name: kasra
letters.sound: Short i: a stroke below.

letters.name: ḍamma
letters.sound: Short u: a small و above.

letters.name: sukūn
letters.sound: Small circle: no vowel after this consonant.

letters.name: shadda
letters.sound: Doubles the consonant: hold it longer.

contrasts.title: س s vs ص ṣ (emphatic)
contrasts.note: Listen to the vowel next to the consonant: emphatics make it sound deeper.

contrasts.title: ع ʕ vs ء ʔ (glottal stop)
ك k vs ق q (MSA)

b.label: ق
b.desc: q, far back in the throat

contrasts.note: This is an MSA contrast (the built-in voice is MSA). In city Shami, ق becomes a glottal stop.

speaking.en: Introduce yourself: your name, where you're from, and what you study.
Greet a friend, ask how they are, answer how you are.
Order something to drink and to eat, politely.
Say three things you do every day.
Say what you like and don't like.
Tell what you did yesterday, in order.
Describe your family: who, how old, where they live.
Describe a friend: name, where from, what they study.
Ask the price of three things and say if they are expensive or cheap.
Tell a doctor what hurts and since when.
Give directions from your dorm to the library.
Say what you will do this weekend and what you must do.
Explain why you are learning Arabic.
Describe your city or campus: big or small, what's there.
Read the MSA reading aloud, then retell it in Levantine.
